text: Teodora Vasquez set the oven to 200 degrees and laid four chicken thighs skin-side up on a sheet pan. The guests were due at seven, and the clock on the microwave read 6:22. She salted the thighs, added sliced lemon and a few sprigs of thyme, and slid the pan onto the middle rack. Next she filled a pot with water for the rice and set it on the back burner. The salad needed only dressing, so she whisked olive oil, mustard, and vinegar in a jar and left it by the bowl. The table already had six plates, six forks, and a folded napkin at each seat. At 6:40 she checked the chicken with a thermometer, which read 61 degrees, and closed the door again. She rinsed the cutting board, dried the knife, and put both back in the drawer.

I started the risotto at half past six because it takes about twenty-five minutes of stirring. The stock was already warm in a saucepan on the left burner, and I ladled it in one cup at a time. My friends had texted that they would arrive around seven. While the rice absorbed the liquid, I grated a block of parmesan into a small bowl and set it next to the stove. The mushrooms were sliced earlier and sat in a colander. I sautéed them in a separate pan with butter and garlic for six minutes, then turned off the heat. My roommate, Bilal, came in and asked whether he should set out glasses. I told him there were eight in the upper cabinet and that we needed five. He counted them out and carried them to the table on a tray.

The recipe card said the lamb shoulder needed three hours, so Haruto Ishikawa had put it in at three in the afternoon. By five-thirty the kitchen smelled of rosemary and cumin. His guests, two colleagues and their partners, were expected at six-fifteen. He took the roasting tin out, basted the meat with the juices, and returned it for the last half hour. On the counter he lined up the side dishes in the order they would be served: flatbread wrapped in a towel, a bowl of yogurt with cucumber, and a tray of roasted carrots. He set a timer on his phone for twenty minutes and wiped down the stovetop. The dishwasher was empty, which meant there would be space for the serving dishes later. He opened a bottle of sparkling water and placed it in the refrigerator door.

I had planned a simple menu: tomato soup, grilled cheese cut into triangles, and a tray of brownies baked that morning. Six people were coming, including two children. At quarter to six I poured the soup from the storage container into a large pot and set the flame to medium. The bread was already buttered on one side and stacked on a plate with slices of cheddar in between. I heated the griddle and tested it with a drop of water, which sizzled and rolled off. The first four sandwiches went on at ten to six. I flipped them after three minutes each. My neighbor, Mrs. Okafor, had lent me two extra chairs, and they were folded against the wall by the door. I unfolded them and placed one at each end of the table.

Siddharth Rao checked the list taped to the refrigerator. It had five items: marinate paneer, chop onions, soak rice, make raita, warm naan. The first four were crossed off. The guests, his cousin and her husband along with three friends from work, would arrive at seven-thirty. He had forty minutes. The paneer had been sitting in yogurt and spices since noon, and he threaded the cubes onto metal skewers along with pieces of green pepper. The grill pan was heating on the largest burner. He cooked the skewers in two batches, turning them every two minutes, and placed them on a platter covered with foil. The rice was simmering under a lid with a cardamom pod and a bay leaf. He wrapped the naan in foil and put it in the low oven to warm.

I opened the fridge and took out the fish fillets that had been thawing since morning. There were four pieces of cod, each about two hundred grams. Dinner was for four, and my sister had said she and her partner would be at the door by seven with their friend Lucía. I patted the fillets dry with paper towels, dusted them with flour, and set them aside on a plate. Then I boiled the potatoes, which were already peeled and cut into quarters, and set a timer for fifteen minutes. A jar of capers and a lemon were on the counter for the sauce. The pan for the fish would only be needed in the last ten minutes, so I wiped it and left it on the stove. I set the table with the blue plates and four glasses.

Grandpa Emeka Nwosu had cooked jollof rice for family gatherings for forty years, and he followed the same order of steps each time. He blended tomatoes, red peppers, and onions into a smooth paste and cooked it down in a heavy pot for twenty minutes. Then he added stock, thyme, curry powder, and two bay leaves. He washed the long-grain rice three times until the water ran clear and stirred it into the pot. The relatives were due at four. At three, he covered the pot with foil and then the lid so the steam would stay in. He fried plantains in a separate pan and drained them on a rack. His granddaughter Adaeze came in from the garden with a bunch of spring onions, and he asked her to slice them thinly for the top.

I timed everything from the guests' arrival backward. They were coming at eight, so the pasta water needed to boil by seven-forty and the sauce needed to be done by seven-thirty. At six-fifty I put the sausage in a wide pan and broke it apart with a wooden spoon. Once it browned, I added chopped fennel and a can of crushed tomatoes and turned the heat down. My partner, Wren, was in the living room moving the coffee table to make space for an extra chair. I called through to ask whether she had found the bread knife, and she said it was in the second drawer. I found it there and sliced the loaf into twelve pieces. Then I set the pot of water on the stove, filled it with salt, and covered it.

The dinner was for eight, and Marguerite Dubois had borrowed a second baking dish from the woman across the hall. She was making two trays of gratin: potatoes sliced thin on a mandoline, layered with cream, garlic, and gruyère. The first tray went into the oven at five-fifteen and the second at five-twenty-five. The guests were arriving at seven. While the gratins baked, she trimmed green beans and dropped them into boiling water for three minutes, then moved them into a bowl of ice water. The roast beef was resting on a board under a sheet of foil. She sliced it at six-forty and arranged the slices on a long white platter. She took a jar of horseradish out of the refrigerator, spooned some into a small dish, and put a teaspoon beside it.

I was making dumplings for six people, and I had folded about sixty of them by four o'clock. They were lined up on two floured trays under damp cloths. The guests, my old roommates from university, were coming at six. The plan was to steam half and pan-fry the other half. I set up the bamboo steamer over a wok with about five centimeters of water and lined each layer with cabbage leaves. For the dipping sauce I mixed soy sauce, black vinegar, a little sugar, and chopped ginger in a measuring cup. At five-thirty I put the first batch in the steamer and set a timer for eight minutes. My friend Joon-ho texted that he was bringing beer and asked if we had a bottle opener. I wrote back that there was one in the drawer by the sink.

Fatima Al-Sayed had laid out the ingredients for the tagine in small bowls before she started: diced lamb, sliced onions, dried apricots, a cinnamon stick, ground ginger, saffron soaking in warm water, and a handful of almonds. The clay pot was on a heat diffuser over a low gas flame. She browned the meat in batches in a separate skillet and moved it into the pot. The guests, her brother's family of four, had said they would come at half past six. She added the onions, the spices, and enough water to come halfway up the meat, then put the conical lid on. It would need ninety minutes. She set a timer and turned to the couscous, which only required boiling water and five minutes of resting. She measured two cups into a bowl and set it by the kettle.

I had not hosted dinner in my new flat before, so I counted the plates first. There were four dinner plates and four side plates, which matched the number of guests if I included myself. The menu was chili, cornbread, and a green salad. The chili had been simmering since four and needed only a final taste for salt. The cornbread batter was in a cast-iron skillet waiting to go into the oven at six-twenty, which would put it on the table at about seven. My coworker Darnell had asked whether he should bring anything, and I suggested a bag of ice. I wiped the counters, emptied the small bin under the sink, and put a fresh liner in it. Then I cut two limes into wedges and put them in a bowl beside a tub of sour cream.

Ingrid Solberg picked up the keys from the building manager at nine on a Saturday. The apartment was on the fourth floor of a brick building in a city she had visited only twice before. The movers were scheduled for eleven. She walked through the rooms with a notebook and wrote down the meter readings for gas and electricity. The kitchen had a two-burner stove, a narrow fridge, and three cabinets. In the bedroom, a radiator sat under the window, and she checked that its valve turned. She measured the space between the closet and the wall to see whether her bookshelf would fit, and it did with five centimeters to spare. When the truck arrived, the movers carried boxes labeled by room. She directed them to set the heavy boxes along the hallway wall.

I arrived in Lisbon with two suitcases and a backpack, and the rest of my things were coming by freight in about ten days. The agent met me outside the building and handed over three keys: one for the street door, one for the apartment, and one for the mailbox. The flat was a one-bedroom on the second floor with tiled floors and tall windows facing a narrow street. She showed me where the water heater switch was and explained that the trash was collected every evening except Sunday. After she left, I unpacked the essentials: a set of sheets, two towels, a kettle, and a phone charger. I walked to the grocery store on the corner and bought bread, eggs, coffee, milk, and dish soap. On the way back I photographed the bus timetable posted at the nearest stop.

The moving van pulled up at the new building at two in the afternoon, and Kwame Asante went upstairs first to prop the door open. His new job started on Monday, and the apartment was a fifteen-minute walk from the office. The unit had a living room, one bedroom, and a small balcony overlooking a parking lot. The movers brought up the mattress, the bed frame in pieces, a desk, two chairs, and twenty-two boxes. Kwame had numbered each box and kept a spreadsheet of contents on his phone. He checked them off as they came through the door. Box fourteen, kitchen utensils, was the last one. After signing the delivery form, he assembled the bed frame with an Allen key and set the mattress on it. Then he plugged in the router the internet company had mailed.

I signed the lease remotely, so the first time I saw the apartment in person was the day I moved in. It matched the photos: a studio with a kitchenette on one wall, a bathroom with a shower stall, and a window above the radiator. The city was six hundred kilometers from where I had lived before. I had driven with a rented trailer, and it took nine hours with two stops for fuel. The landlord, Mr. Petrov, met me at the curb and walked me through the building rules, which were printed on a single page. Recycling went in the blue bins behind the building, and quiet hours started at ten. I unloaded the trailer in about forty minutes. The futon frame went against the long wall, and the small table went under the window.

Paloma Ruiz had three weeks between leaving her old job and starting the new one, and she used the first two days to set up the apartment. On the first morning she went to the city office to register her address, which required her passport, the rental contract, and a form she had downloaded the night before. The clerk stamped the form and handed back a printed confirmation. Next she went to the bank to update her address and to the phone shop to get a local SIM card. In the afternoon she opened the boxes marked kitchen and bathroom. She lined the drawers with paper, arranged plates on the lower shelf, and put the shower curtain on its rod. Before evening she made a list of furniture she still needed: a lamp, a rug, and curtains.

I took the overnight train with my bicycle and three duffel bags, and I reached the new city at seven in the morning. The apartment was a shared flat with two other tenants, and my room was the one at the end of the corridor. One of the flatmates, Annika, was making coffee when I came in. She showed me the shelf in the fridge that was mine, the rota for cleaning the bathroom, and the code for the Wi-Fi. My room had a bed, a wardrobe, a desk, and a chair. I emptied the duffel bags into the wardrobe, putting shirts on hangers and folding the rest onto the shelves. The bicycle went into the storage room in the basement, which had hooks on the wall. I locked it to a pipe with a chain and returned upstairs.

Rohan Mehta's company had arranged a relocation service, so a coordinator named Ms. Lindqvist met him at the airport and drove him to the apartment. On the way she gave him a folder containing the lease, the building's contact list, a map of the neighborhood, and instructions for setting up utilities. The apartment was furnished, with a sofa, a dining table, a bed, and a small washing machine in the kitchen. She explained that the heating was controlled by a thermostat in the hallway and that it was set to twenty degrees. Rohan unpacked his clothes and laid out his laptop on the dining table. In the afternoon he walked to the supermarket two blocks away and bought rice, lentils, onions, tomatoes, and a box of tea. He then found the laundromat noted on the map.

The new apartment was on the ground floor, which made the move easier. I had hired two students through an online listing to help me carry things from the truck. It took them an hour and a half to bring everything inside, including a washing machine on a hand dolly. I paid them in cash and they left. The kitchen faced the back courtyard, and the bedroom faced the street. I measured the windows for blinds and wrote the numbers on the back of an envelope: ninety by one hundred forty for the kitchen, one hundred twenty by one hundred sixty for the bedroom. In the evening I connected the washing machine to the water inlet and ran an empty cycle to test the drain. Then I set up the bed and put the boxes of books in the corner.

Aiyana Whitehorse arrived in the city on a Thursday and spent the night in a hotel because her lease began on Friday. In the morning she checked out, took a taxi to the building, and collected the keys from a lockbox using a four-digit code the property company had emailed. The apartment was on the sixth floor and had an elevator. She walked through every room with her phone and recorded a video of the walls, floors, and appliances for the move-in inspection. There was a small scratch on the kitchen counter and a missing cover on one electrical outlet, and she wrote both down on the inspection form. The movers called to say they would arrive at one. In the meantime she wiped the shelves and put a new roll of paper in the bathroom.

I moved from a small town to a city of about two million people, and the first practical problem was transit. The apartment was near a tram line, so on my first day I bought a monthly pass at a machine on the platform. It cost forty-nine euros and was valid from the first to the last day of the month. Then I took the tram to a furniture store at the end of the line and ordered a wardrobe, a desk, and a bookcase, all to be delivered the following Tuesday. The clerk, a man named Gerhard, wrote my address on the order form and asked for a phone number. On the way back I stopped at a hardware store and bought a drill bit set, wall plugs, a level, and a box of screws.

Chen Yuqing's apartment came with an empty kitchen, so the first purchases were a pot, a frying pan, a cutting board, a knife, and a set of bowls. She bought them at a market three streets from the building on the afternoon she arrived. The building was older, with six floors and no elevator, and her unit was on the fifth. She carried the boxes up in four trips. The previous tenant had left a desk and a lamp, which the landlord said she could keep. She set up her laptop on the desk and called the internet provider, who gave her an installation slot for Monday between nine and noon. Until then she would use the data on her phone. In the evening she cooked noodles with spinach and an egg and washed the new bowls afterward.

I drove the last two hundred kilometers on a Sunday and reached the apartment just after four. The building superintendent, Mr. Abernathy, lived on the ground floor and had my keys in an envelope with my name on it. He walked me up to the third floor and pointed out the fuse box in the hallway closet and the shut-off valve under the kitchen sink. The apartment had hardwood floors, a gas range, and a window unit for cooling. My furniture was arriving with a moving company on Tuesday, so for two nights I would sleep on an inflatable mattress. I pumped it up with the electric pump that came with it and laid a sleeping bag on top. Then I unpacked the toiletries, hung a towel in the bathroom, and set the alarm for seven.

At the twenty-five mile marker, Tomasz Kowalczyk looked at his watch. It read three hours and thirty-one minutes. He had planned to finish around three forty-two, which meant he needed to hold his pace of eight minutes and twenty seconds per mile. The course in this section ran along the river on a flat asphalt path. Volunteers at a water station held out paper cups, and he took one, drank half, and dropped the cup into a bin. His left shoelace had loosened, but it was still tied, so he left it. Spectators stood behind metal barriers on both sides. A sign announced one mile remaining. He passed a runner in a yellow shirt and settled behind a small group moving at the same speed. The road turned left onto a wide avenue lined with flags.

I reached the last mile at around four hours and five minutes. My plan had been to walk through the final water station and then run the rest without stopping, so that is what I did. A volunteer handed me a cup of electrolyte drink, and I finished it in three sips. The course went up a short incline past a church and then flattened out. My watch beeped at twenty-five miles, and I checked my heart rate, which was 162. I shortened my stride on the hill and kept my arms low. There were people cheering along the route, and someone read my name off my bib and called it out. Ahead I could see the overhead banner of the finish area. I moved to the right side of the road, where the surface was smoother, and kept going.

Mariam Haddad had trained for sixteen weeks for this race, following a plan that peaked at a twenty-mile run three weeks before. Now, in the final mile, the plan called for her to use whatever pace she had left. Her watch showed nine minutes and ten seconds for mile twenty-five. The course passed a row of shops and turned onto a bridge, where the wind came from the right. She tucked in behind a taller runner for a few hundred meters to stay out of it. At the end of the bridge, a timing mat beeped under her shoes. The crowd was thicker here, and a band was playing on a small stage. She took the last energy gel from her waist belt, tore it open, and squeezed it out while running. The finish clock was visible around the next corner.

With a mile to go, I did the math on my time. I had crossed the half at one hour fifty-four, and I was now at three hours forty-nine. If I ran the last 1.2 miles in eleven minutes, I would finish under four hours. That was the number I had written on the back of my hand that morning. My legs were heavy, and my right calf had been tight since mile twenty, so I kept my stride short and my cadence steady. The course went down a gentle slope toward the waterfront. A man next to me, wearing a shirt that said Running Club Accra, asked what time we were on, and I told him. He nodded and kept pace beside me for a while. The last turn came, and I could see the finishing gantry.

The final mile of the city marathon passed through the old market district, and Lars Eriksen had studied the route map the night before. He knew there were two turns, a short climb, and then a straight of about six hundred meters to the line. His time at mile twenty-five was three hours and two minutes. He had been running alongside the same three people since mile twenty-two. At the first turn, one of them dropped back. Lars kept his eyes on the curb line and stepped over a discarded water bottle. On the climb he leaned forward slightly and pumped his arms. A medical tent was set up at the top with two paramedics standing beside it. When the road leveled out, he lengthened his stride. The finish clock read three hours eleven minutes as he approached it.

My coach had told me to treat the last mile like a separate race. At the twenty-five mile sign, I pressed the lap button on my watch so I could see the pace for just that stretch. The course went through a park with a gravel path, and the surface shifted under my shoes. I ran on the edge where it was more compact. A runner in front of me had stopped to stretch her hamstring against a tree. I passed her and checked the lap pace: eight minutes and forty-five seconds per mile. The path came out of the park onto a closed road with barriers on both sides. There were mile markers every quarter mile in the last stretch, and I counted them. At the last one, a sign read 400 meters, and the finish arch was directly ahead.

Yusuf Demir was sixty-two years old, and this was his eleventh marathon. He ran the last mile the way he always did, at an even pace without a final sprint. His split for mile twenty-five was ten minutes and thirty seconds. The course in this section followed a wide boulevard lined with plane trees. He took a cup of water from a table, poured half over his head, and drank the rest. Near the twenty-six mile marker, a photographer crouched on a step stool, and Yusuf glanced at the lens as he passed. His granddaughter Elif was supposed to be waiting at the barrier just before the finish. He looked along the line of spectators on the left side and saw her standing next to a lamp post with a jacket over her arm. He crossed the line at four hours fifty-three.

The last mile of the course was along a stretch of beach road, and the wind was coming straight off the water. I had passed the twenty-five mile marker at three hours and twenty-eight minutes. I adjusted my cap so it wouldn't blow off and moved to the inside of a group of five runners. We stayed together for about half a mile, rotating so different people were at the front. My watch vibrated every kilometer, and at forty-one kilometers it showed a split of five minutes and two seconds. The road curved inland past a parking lot and a row of beach huts. Volunteers in orange vests stood at intervals with megaphones, telling runners to keep left. The finish was in a square near the old harbor, and the timing gantry stood at the far end.

Nomvula Dlamini wore a pace band on her wrist with target splits printed for every mile. In the last mile, the band said she should be at three hours fifty-three when she passed mile twenty-five, and her watch said three fifty-four. She was one minute behind the plan. The road was closed to traffic and lined with cones, and the surface was smooth. She shortened her steps on a slight downhill to keep her quads from taking too much load. At the twenty-six mile sign, an announcer was reading out names and hometowns over loudspeakers. She heard a few names before hers but not her own. The final 385 yards were on a carpeted section with sponsor boards on each side. She looked up at the clock above the line, which showed four hours and three minutes.

I was running the last mile with a stomach cramp on my right side that had started at mile twenty-four. I slowed my breathing and pressed two fingers into the spot below my ribs, which a training partner had once suggested. After a few minutes it eased. The course went through a residential street where people had set up tables with orange slices and pretzels. I took two orange slices from a boy holding out a plate. At the end of the street the route turned onto the main road, and the barriers began. My watch said I had run 25.6 miles, slightly more than the official distance because of the turns I had taken wide. I kept to the blue line painted on the road, which marked the shortest route. The finish came after one more bend.

Rafael Moreno had run the first twenty-five miles of the marathon at a steady pace, and in the last mile he started passing people. His watch showed his pace dropping from eight minutes thirty per mile to eight minutes ten. The course was flat and ran along a canal with a towpath on one side. A boat with a camera crew moved alongside the runners for a few hundred meters. Rafael pulled his sunglasses down from his forehead because the sun had come out from behind the clouds. At the final aid station he skipped the water and kept running. The barriers narrowed the course to two lanes, and a volunteer pointed runners to the right lane for the full marathon finish and the left lane for the relay. Rafael took the right lane and crossed the mat.

It was my first marathon, and by the last mile I had stopped looking at my watch. The course ran through the university campus, past the library and the stadium. I knew from the map that the finish was on the athletics track inside the stadium. The road sloped down into a tunnel under the stands, and it was darker and cooler for about fifty meters. When I came out, I was on the track, and the finish line was on the far side, about three hundred meters away. Runners ahead of me were spread out around the curve. I stayed in lane one. A volunteer at the line held a stack of foil blankets, and another was handing out medals on ribbons. I crossed the line, stopped my watch, and took a blanket and a bottle of water.

Dolores Mendoza let her terrier, Pico, out into the back yard at eight in the evening, as she did every night. Usually he scratched at the door after about five minutes. At eight-twenty she noticed he had not come back. She put on her shoes, took the flashlight from the hook by the door, and went out. The yard was about fifteen meters deep, with a wooden fence on three sides and a shed in the far corner. She swept the light along the fence line and found a gap at the bottom of one panel where the soil had washed away. On the other side was her neighbor's garden. She walked around the block to the neighbor's front door and rang the bell. The neighbor, Mr. Harlan, came out with her and found Pico under his porch steps.

I opened the back door at ten to call Biscuit in, and she did not come. She is a nine-year-old beagle, and she normally waits on the step. I switched on the outdoor light, which covers about half the yard. The gate was latched. I walked to the back corner, where there is a compost bin and a row of tomato plants, and called her name twice. Then I heard rustling under the deck. I knelt down, pointed my phone flashlight through the slats, and saw her lying on her side next to a tennis ball that had rolled there weeks ago. The gap between the deck and the ground is narrow, so I went to the side where the lattice panel is loose, pulled it back, and she crawled out with the ball in her mouth.

Kenji Watanabe had let the dog out after dinner and gone back to washing dishes. When he finished, about twenty minutes later, he realized the dog, a shiba named Momo, had not barked at the door. He dried his hands and checked the yard from the kitchen window, but the light from the house did not reach the far end. He took a headlamp from the drawer and went outside. The yard was rectangular, with a hedge along the back and a chain-link fence on the sides. He walked the perimeter, shining the light at the base of the hedge. Halfway along he found a hole about the width of a dinner plate, freshly dug. He went to the front of the house, got into the car, and drove slowly down the street with the window open.

It was raining lightly when I let our retriever, Juniper, out at six in the morning. I made coffee and checked the news on my phone, and by the time I looked up, fifteen minutes had passed. She hadn't come back in. I went to the back door and whistled the two-note whistle we use for recall. Nothing. I put on a raincoat and walked out. The grass was wet and there were muddy paw prints leading toward the side of the garage. Behind the garage there is a narrow strip where we store the recycling bins and a stack of firewood. She was standing there with her nose in a gap between two logs. I looked closer and saw a hedgehog curled into a ball. I clipped the leash to her collar and walked her back inside.

Priya Nair's dog, a mixed breed called Toast, had been in the yard for an hour. Priya was on a work call and had left the door open a crack so he could come in when he wanted. After the call ended, she checked his bed in the living room and found it empty. She went outside. The yard had a low wall at the back, about a meter high, and a flower bed along one side. She checked behind the barbecue and under the table on the patio. Then she looked over the wall into the alley that ran behind the row of houses. Toast was there, sitting next to a delivery van, while the driver, a man in a gray uniform, unloaded boxes. Priya called his name, walked around through the side gate, and took hold of his collar.

We have a sensor on the dog door that logs every time it opens, and when I checked the app at eleven, the last entry was 10:12, outbound. That meant Rufus, our basset hound, had been outside for almost an hour. I went to the back door and turned on the floodlight. Our yard slopes downward to a stream at the bottom, and there is a fence before the water. I walked down the slope and found the fence intact. Then I heard snoring. Rufus was asleep on a pile of leaves under the large oak tree, about five meters from the fence. He had probably gone out to sniff around and then lay down. I woke him by tapping his side, and he got up slowly. We walked back up to the house together and I closed the dog door for the night.

Aleksander Nowak lived on a farm, and his sheepdog, Bryn, usually came back to the porch by dusk. On this evening the sun had set at half past seven, and by eight the dog was not there. Aleksander took a lantern from the barn and walked to the lower field, where the sheep were kept. The gate to the field was closed. He walked along the stone wall and called once. A short bark came from the far corner near the water trough. When he reached it, he found Bryn standing beside a ewe that had gotten her back leg caught in a coil of old wire. Aleksander set the lantern on the wall, took a pair of pliers from his jacket, and cut the wire in two places. The ewe stood up and walked off toward the flock.

I let my grandmother's poodle, Coco, into the yard while I cleaned the kitchen. I was staying at her house for the week while she visited my uncle. After about ten minutes I went to the back door to let Coco in, and she wasn't on the step. The yard was small and fully fenced, with a rose bed along the back and a birdbath in the middle. I looked behind the rose bushes and under the bench. Then I noticed the side gate was open about twenty centimeters. The latch had not caught properly. I walked out to the front of the house and looked up and down the street. Coco was two doors down, sitting on the neighbor's front lawn, where a woman was watering plants. She said Coco had come over a few minutes earlier.

Obinna Eze checked the time when he realized the dog had not come in. It was 9:40 p.m., and he had let her out at 9:15. The dog, a large German shepherd named Kira, normally stayed within sight of the back door. He went outside with a flashlight. The yard had a tall wooden fence and a gate with a padlock, which was still locked. He called her name and listened. There was a scraping sound from the far corner. When he got there, he found Kira digging at the base of the fence, where a rabbit burrow went under the boards. Only her back half was visible. He took hold of her collar and pulled her back gently. Then he took two bricks from the stack beside the shed and placed them over the hole to block it.

My dog, Pepper, is twelve and partially deaf, so when she does not come in, I usually have to go get her. On Tuesday night she had been out for about fifteen minutes. I stepped onto the patio with a flashlight and swept it across the lawn. She was not on the grass. I checked the vegetable garden, which is enclosed with chicken wire, and she was not there either. Then I remembered that she sometimes goes into the shed when the door is left open, because there is an old blanket on the floor. The shed door was open. I shone the light inside, and she was lying on the blanket next to the lawnmower. I clapped twice near her so she would feel the vibration through the floor, and she stood up and followed me.

Hyun-woo Park lived in a townhouse with a small walled courtyard, and his corgi, Dubu, usually spent his evenings there. At ten o'clock Hyun-woo opened the sliding door and called him. No dog appeared. He stepped outside. The courtyard was paved and had several large potted plants, a bicycle leaning against the wall, and a table with two chairs. He looked behind each pot. Then he noticed that the bicycle had been moved and that a wooden panel leaning against the wall had fallen flat. Underneath the panel there was a gap leading to the neighbor's courtyard. He knocked on the neighbor's door, and an older man named Mr. Seo answered and said Dubu had been in his courtyard for about twenty minutes, eating fallen persimmons. He handed the dog back over the wall.

The dog had been outside since lunch, and at three o'clock I noticed the water bowl on the patio was still full. That was unusual, so I went to look. Our yard is large, about half an acre, with a fence along the road and woods along the back. The dog, a husky named Sitka, often lies in the shade under the pine trees. I walked over there, and she wasn't in her usual spot. I checked the fence along the road for gaps. The gate was closed and the fence was whole. At the edge of the woods, I found her collar tag lying in the grass, which meant the ring had broken. I followed a narrow deer path for about thirty meters and found her lying beside a creek. I clipped a spare leash to her harness and led her back.

Ezekiel Thornton tuned his cello in the green room at a quarter to eight. The recital was scheduled for eight, and the program listed him second, after a pianist who would play two Chopin études. He checked the A string against the electronic tuner on his phone and then tuned the other strings in fifths by ear. His music was in a black folder, with the pages taped together so he would not need a page turn in the first movement. He rosined his bow with six even strokes. A stage manager with a headset came in and told him the hall was about three-quarters full and that the house lights would go down in five minutes. Ezekiel took the endpin holder out of his case, put it in his jacket pocket, and stood by the door to the wings.

I was the drummer for a four-piece band playing a bar on a Friday night, and we were on at ten. The sound engineer had done a line check at nine-fifteen. My kit was set up at the back of the stage on a rug so the bass drum would not slide. I checked the tension on the snare and tightened two lugs a quarter turn each. Then I adjusted the hi-hat clutch, which had loosened during load-in. The set list was taped to the floor beside my throne: twelve songs, starting with a mid-tempo one at 112 beats per minute. I tapped the tempo on my thigh and checked it against the metronome app. Our singer, Marisol, came over and asked if I had spare sticks. I pointed to the stick bag hanging on the floor tom.

The school concert started at six-thirty, and Ama Owusu was the fourth performer, playing a piece for solo flute. She sat in the second row of chairs set aside for performers, holding the flute across her knees. The program, printed on a single folded sheet, listed her name and the title: Syrinx by Debussy. She knew the piece took about three minutes. When the third performer, a boy playing the trumpet, finished, the music teacher announced her name. Ama walked to the center of the stage, where a music stand was already set at her height. She put her sheet music on the stand, though she had memorized the piece, and adjusted the headjoint of her flute slightly. She looked at the teacher, who nodded from the side of the stage. Then she took a breath and began.

I play keyboard in a church band, and every Sunday we have the same routine. We arrive at eight-thirty for a nine-thirty service. I switched on the keyboard and the amplifier and checked the settings: piano sound on the lower split, strings on the upper split, volume at seventy percent. The worship leader, Brother Tobias, handed out the song list, which had five songs and the keys written next to each title. Two were in G, two in D, and one in E-flat. I wrote the chord charts into my tablet and set the page-turn pedal under my left foot. At nine-fifteen the sound technician asked us to play a few bars of the first song so he could balance the levels. Then we stood near our instruments while people came in and took their seats.

Valentina Russo stood in the wings of the opera house with her score held under her arm. She was singing the role of the Countess, and her first entrance was at the beginning of Act Two. The first act had just ended, and the stage crew was moving furniture into position for the bedroom scene: a chaise, a dressing table, and a tall screen. A dresser adjusted the hooks at the back of her gown and pinned a stray curl under her wig. Valentina drank a few sips of water from a bottle with a sports cap so the liquid would not spill on her costume. The stage manager called places over the backstage speaker. The lights went to blue, and she walked onto the stage in the dark and took her position on the chaise.

I was playing guitar at an open mic night in a café, and my name was seventh on the list. Each performer had ten minutes, which meant I had about an hour before my turn. I sat at a table near the side and drank a cup of mint tea. My guitar was in a soft case leaning against the wall. When the fifth performer started, I took the guitar out and tuned it with a clip-on tuner. I put a capo on the second fret for the first song and placed a spare pick in my shirt pocket. The host, a woman named Gwendolyn, checked her clipboard and nodded at me to get ready. When the sixth performer finished, I carried my guitar to the stool, plugged the cable into the jack, and lowered the microphone stand.

The jazz trio was booked for two sets at a hotel lounge, and Ibrahim Diallo played upright bass. They started at nine. At eight-thirty he carried the bass in from the car, laid it on its side, and took it out of its padded cover. He checked the strings for wear and wiped the fingerboard with a cloth. The pickup cable ran to a small amplifier that he set on a stand so it would project above the audience's chairs. The pianist, a man named Florian, played a few chords so they could check the balance. Ibrahim turned the amplifier's bass knob down a notch. The drummer set a short list of tunes on the piano: four standards for the first set, starting with a medium swing in F. At nine, the lounge manager signaled, and they began.

I was performing a solo piano recital at a public library as part of a monthly series. The library had a grand piano in a reading room, and folding chairs had been set up for about forty people. I arrived an hour early to try the instrument. The action was slightly heavier than my piano at home, and the left pedal squeaked when pressed halfway. I told the librarian, and she brought a small can of lubricant from the maintenance closet, which helped. I played through the first page of each piece to get used to the touch. The program had four pieces and would last about forty minutes. At two o'clock, the librarian introduced me and read a short biography from a card. I sat down, adjusted the bench by turning the knobs on both sides, and began the first piece.

Thandiwe Mokoena was the lead vocalist for a choir performing at a community hall, and she had a solo verse in the third song. The choir had forty members, arranged in three rows on risers. Before the concert, the director, Mr. Van der Berg, gave everyone the starting pitches using a pitch pipe and reminded them to watch for the cutoff at the end of each phrase. Thandiwe stood in the front row, second from the left, holding a black folder with the music. During the first two songs she sang with the altos. At the start of the third, she stepped forward to a microphone on a stand that had been placed at the edge of the risers. The pianist played four bars of introduction, and she counted them silently before starting her verse.

I was the second violinist in a string quartet playing at a wedding reception, and we were set up in the corner of a garden marquee. The program had been agreed with the couple a month earlier: twenty pieces for the drinks reception, mostly arrangements of pop songs and some Vivaldi. We had clips on our music stands because there was a breeze coming through the open side of the tent. Before we started, I tuned to the first violinist's A and then checked my strings in fifths. The cellist, Oyelaran, had brought an extension cord for a small light that clipped onto his stand. At four o'clock the wedding coordinator came over and said the guests were coming out from the ceremony. We started with the first piece on the list, a Pachelbel arrangement.

The festival's stage manager gave the electronic duo a fifteen-minute changeover. Freya Lindgren and her partner, Moses, had their equipment packed onto two rolling carts: a laptop, two controllers, a small mixer, a synthesizer, and a bundle of cables tied with velcro straps. Freya set the laptop on the table and connected it to the mixer while Moses ran the stereo outputs to the stage snake. The house engineer gave them a thumbs-up when the signal appeared on his board. They checked their in-ear monitors by playing a few seconds of the opening track. Freya looked at the set timer on the side of the stage, which read three minutes to start. She opened the project file, checked that the tempo was set to 124, and placed her hand on the controller's first fader.

I was about to play a tuba solo with a community wind band at an outdoor concert in a park. The band was seated in a semicircle under a bandstand roof, and the audience sat on blankets and lawn chairs on the grass. My solo was in the fourth piece, a march, and it lasted sixteen bars. The conductor, Ms. Castellanos-Reid, had told me to stand for it. I emptied the water from the tuning slides during the applause after the third piece by pressing the water keys and blowing air through. When the march began, I counted the measures on my fingers. At bar thirty-two, I stood up, lifted the bell slightly, and played the solo at the marked dynamic. Then I sat down and joined the rest of the low brass for the trio section.

When Benedikt Hauser came home from work, there was a cardboard box on the doormat, about the size of a shoebox, wrapped in brown tape. The label had his name and address printed on it, but the return address was a warehouse in a town he did not recognize. He had not ordered anything recently. He carried the box inside, set it on the kitchen table, and cut the tape with a pair of scissors. Inside, packed in shredded paper, was a ceramic mug with a blue glaze and a printed card. The card said the mug was a gift from his colleague Ottilie, sent through an online shop, with a note thanking him for covering her shifts in October. He rinsed the mug, dried it with a towel, and put it on the shelf with the others.

I found a padded envelope in my mailbox on Wednesday with a customs sticker on the front. It had come from Japan, and the declaration listed the contents as printed matter, value twelve dollars. I had not ordered anything from Japan. I opened it at the kitchen counter. Inside were two paperback books in Japanese and a postcard. The postcard was from my cousin Akiko, who had moved to Osaka the year before. She wrote that she had found the books at a secondhand store and thought I might use them for my language classes. One was a book of short stories and the other was a children's dictionary with illustrations. I put the books on my desk next to my notebook and pinned the postcard to the corkboard above it.

The courier rang the bell at ten in the morning and handed Lucinda Barros a large flat box, which she signed for on a handheld device. It was addressed to her but had no sender name, only the logo of a furniture company. She checked her email for an order confirmation and found none. She opened the box on the living room floor. Inside was a flat-packed side table in pale wood, with a bag of screws, four legs, and an instruction sheet. Taped to the top was an invoice showing that the order had been placed by her brother, Duarte, with a message field reading: for the hallway. She remembered mentioning the empty hallway on a phone call. She found an Allen key in the bag and assembled the table in about fifteen minutes.

I wasn't expecting anything, so when the post office left a slip saying a parcel was waiting for collection, I assumed it was a mistake. I took the slip and my ID to the branch on Saturday morning. The clerk scanned the slip, went into the back, and came out with a box about thirty centimeters on each side. The label was handwritten in blue ink, and the sender was listed as T. Gallagher, with an address in Galway. That was my great-aunt Theresa. At home I opened the box. It contained a knitted scarf in gray wool, a jar of homemade blackberry jam wrapped in newspaper, and a short letter. The letter said she was clearing out a cupboard and had more jam than she needed. I put the jam in the pantry.

Dimitri Papadopoulos found a small box wedged into the mail slot of his apartment door. It was addressed to him, but the sender's name was a company he had never heard of. He opened it at the desk. Inside was a fitness tracker in a plastic tray and a letter explaining that he had been selected as a test user for a new model. The letter asked him to wear the device for thirty days and complete a short online survey each week. A prepaid return envelope was included for sending it back afterward. Dimitri searched the company name online and found that it was a subsidiary of a larger electronics manufacturer and that the program was real. He charged the device using the USB cable in the box and fastened it to his left wrist.

A package arrived for me at the office, and the receptionist brought it to my desk. It was a long tube, the kind used for posters, with an international shipping label from Canada. I didn't know anyone who had a reason to send me something from there. I pulled off the plastic end cap and slid out a rolled print. It was a topographic map of a national park in British Columbia, printed on heavy paper. A business card was clipped to the corner. It belonged to Gord MacIntyre, a hiking guide I had emailed a year earlier with a question about a trail. On the back he had written that the shop was clearing old stock and that he remembered my question about the northern route. I took the map home and measured it for a frame.

Saanvi Kapoor opened her mailbox and found a slip of paper telling her a package had been left with the neighbor in 3B. She knocked on the door, and the neighbor, an older man named Mr. Brennan, handed her a box with a bookstore's logo printed on the side. It was heavy for its size. Saanvi had not ordered any books that month. Upstairs, she cut the tape and found three hardcover cookbooks and a gift receipt. The receipt was for an order made by her former roommate, Ingeborg, who had written a note in the gift message field: for your birthday, sent a bit late. Saanvi's birthday had been two weeks earlier. She stacked the books on the kitchen shelf next to the spice rack and opened the one on Ethiopian cooking to the table of contents.

I got home and found a box on the porch addressed to the previous owner of the house, a Mrs. Wilhelmina Strand. We had bought the house four months earlier. The box was from a seed company and had a perforated window showing several small paper packets inside. I checked the old forwarding information the real estate agent had given us, which included a new address for Mrs. Strand in a retirement community about thirty kilometers away. I wrote return to sender on the box and then crossed it out, because the post office would take longer than driving it over myself. On Saturday I drove to the retirement community, signed in at the front desk, and asked the receptionist to pass the box along. She took it and wrote the room number on a sticky note.

Tariq Aziz received a package that had been mailed to the wrong apartment number. It was addressed to a T. Aziz in unit 14, but he lived in unit 41. The building manager had matched the name and left it at his door. He opened it before noticing the number. Inside were two pairs of running shoes, one in size forty-two and one in size thirty-eight, with a packing slip. He had not ordered shoes. He took the box down to the lobby and checked the mailbox directory. Unit 14 was listed under the name Tahira Aziz. He went to the fourteenth unit and knocked. A woman answered, and he explained that the box had been delivered to him by mistake and that he had opened it. She checked the slip, confirmed the order, and took the box.

On Monday a box from a wine shop was left at my door, and I had to show ID to the delivery driver, who checked my date of birth before handing it over. It contained six bottles separated by cardboard dividers and an envelope. The envelope held a card from the firm where I had done freelance work over the summer, thanking me for the project and listing the wines: two reds from Rioja, two whites from the Loire, and two bottles of cava. I hadn't known they were sending anything. I put the whites and the cava in the refrigerator and the reds on the rack by the pantry. Then I sent a short email to my contact at the firm, a project manager named Henrike, to confirm that the shipment had arrived in good condition.

The parcel was on the step when Celestine Bouchard came back from the market. It was a sturdy cardboard box, about the size of a microwave, with fragile stickers on two sides. The sender was listed as a ceramics studio in Quebec. Celestine had not placed an order. She brought it inside and set it on the floor. Under a layer of bubble wrap, she found a large serving bowl with a speckled green glaze and an envelope taped to the inside flap. The note was from her nephew, Laurent, who had taken a pottery course over the winter. He wrote that the bowl had come out of the kiln with a slight warp on one side, so it would sit level only on a flat surface. Celestine placed it in the center of the dining table and checked that it did not rock.

Last Thursday I received a package from my own bank. It was a small box with the bank's logo, sent by registered mail, and I had to sign for it. I hadn't requested anything from them. Inside was a hardware security key, a small device that plugs into a USB port, along with a letter. The letter said the bank was replacing text message verification with physical keys for all business account holders and that the old method would end on the first of next month. There was a setup guide with six steps. I followed them on my laptop: logged in, went to the security settings, selected the option to register a key, plugged it in, touched the gold contact, and named it. The site confirmed the registration, and I put the spare key in the desk drawer.

The three Okonkwo siblings met at their grandmother's house on a Saturday to go through her belongings before the property was sold. Chiamaka, the eldest, brought a roll of colored stickers: red for keep, blue for donate, yellow for sell. Her brothers, Ikenna and Uche, started in the living room. There was a sideboard, a glass-fronted cabinet with porcelain figurines, two armchairs, and a rug. Chiamaka listed each item in a notebook as they decided. Ikenna wanted the sideboard for his dining room and put a red sticker on it. The figurines went into a box marked donate, each wrapped in newspaper. Uche took photographs of the armchairs to post on a local sale site. By noon they had finished the living room and moved to the kitchen, where the cupboards held about forty plates.

My sister and I spent Sunday going through our grandmother's closet. She had died in March, and her apartment had to be returned to the housing association by the end of the month. We emptied the wardrobe onto the bed first. There were eleven coats, about thirty blouses, and a shelf of folded sweaters. My sister, Ottavia, suggested that we check every pocket before bagging anything, and she found a bus ticket from 1987, two handkerchiefs, and a folded receipt for a pair of shoes. We sorted the clothing into charity bags and set aside two scarves and a wool coat that we each wanted. At the bottom of the wardrobe there were six shoeboxes. Five held shoes. The sixth held letters tied with string, which we put in a separate bag to read later.

Gabriel and Inés Castillo started in the attic of their grandmother's house because it held the most boxes. The attic was reached by a pull-down ladder in the hallway, and there was a single light bulb with a chain switch. Gabriel handed the boxes down to Inés, who stacked them in the hallway. There were twenty-three. They opened them one at a time on the dining table. Several contained Christmas decorations, each ornament wrapped in tissue paper. One held old tax records, which Inés checked against a list from the lawyer and then put in a bag for shredding. Another contained a sewing machine in its original case, with the manual and a box of bobbins. Gabriel wrote the contents of each box on a sheet of paper, and they decided item by item what would go where.

My brothers and I divided our grandmother's books among us. She had about four hundred, on six shelves in her study, and most were history and travel. We agreed on a system: we would take turns choosing one book each, starting with the youngest, until each of us had what we wanted, and the rest would go to the public library's book sale. My youngest brother, Sacha, chose first and took an atlas from 1962. I took a three-volume history of the Ottoman Empire. My older brother, Mattias, took a guide to the birds of Northern Europe. We went around twelve times before we stopped. I carried the remaining books out to the car in banana boxes from the supermarket, nine boxes in total, and drove them to the library's loading dock before it closed at five.

When Hana Novak and her brother Pavel sorted their grandmother's kitchen, they found that she had kept the original box for nearly every appliance. The mixer, the toaster, the coffee grinder, and a food processor each sat in its box on the top shelf of the pantry, with the manual and receipt inside. Hana said that would make it easy to sell them. Pavel set them on the table and tested each one by plugging it in. The mixer and the grinder worked. The toaster's left slot did not heat. They put the working items in one pile and the toaster in the recycling pile. In the drawers they found cutlery, a set of cookie cutters in the shape of animals, and a notebook of handwritten recipes. Pavel photographed each page of the notebook with his phone.

My cousin and I sorted through Grandma Rosalind's garage, which she had used mainly for storage after she stopped driving. There was a workbench along one wall, a set of metal shelves along another, and a lawnmower in the corner. My cousin, Wendell, worked on the shelves while I worked on the bench. The bench drawers held screws sorted by size into baby food jars, each labeled in marker. There was a hand drill, a set of chisels, and a tape measure. Wendell found gardening tools, three bags of potting soil, and a box of clay pots on the shelves. We loaded the tools we wanted into the trunks of our cars and put the rest on the driveway with a sign that said free. By three o'clock the lawnmower and the clay pots were gone.

The lawyer had sent the siblings an inventory of the house's contents, and Ngozi, Femi, and Tolu Adeyemi used it as a checklist. Each of them had marked the items they wanted beforehand, and there were only three overlaps. They met at the house to settle those. The first was a clock that hung in the hallway. Femi and Tolu had both marked it. They flipped a coin, and Tolu took it. The second was a set of silver serving spoons, which they divided into three sets of four. The third was a framed photograph of the house taken in 1974, which Ngozi suggested they have reprinted so each could have a copy. She took the frame off the wall, removed the print, and put it in an envelope to take to a photo shop.

I sorted the jewelry box with my two sisters at our grandmother's dressing table. The box had three tiers and a small drawer at the bottom. We took everything out and laid it on a white towel so the pieces would not roll. There were nine rings, five necklaces, two brooches, a wristwatch with a leather strap, and a handful of single earrings without partners. My sister Leilani had arranged for a jeweler to appraise the pieces the following week, so we wrote a numbered list and photographed each item next to a ruler. The wristwatch had stopped at a quarter past four. My other sister, Kalena, wound it, and it started ticking. We put everything back into the box in the same order as the list and wrote the numbers on small paper tags.

Arjun and Meera Pillai went through their grandmother's papers in the spare bedroom, where she had kept a filing cabinet with four drawers. The top drawer held bank statements and utility bills going back fifteen years. The second held medical records and insurance documents. The third held property papers, including the deed to the house and a survey map from 1981. The fourth held personal correspondence, sorted into folders by year. Arjun set up a laptop and a portable scanner on the bed. Meera passed him documents from the second and third drawers, and he scanned anything the lawyer's checklist mentioned. The rest of the financial papers went into bags for a shredding service, which would collect them on Tuesday. They left the correspondence folders in the fourth drawer and moved the whole cabinet into Meera's car.

We spent two days on our grandmother's sewing room. My brother Ruairí and I took the first day, and our sister Clodagh joined on the second. The room had a sewing machine on a table, a chest of drawers full of fabric, and a wall of shelves holding jars of buttons, spools of thread, and patterns in envelopes. We measured the fabric pieces with a tape measure and wrote the dimensions on masking tape stuck to each one. Anything over a meter went into one bin and smaller pieces went into another. A quilting group from the local church had agreed to take both bins. The patterns were mostly from the 1970s, and Clodagh found a website that collects them, so we packed those separately. The sewing machine went to Clodagh, who had space for it.

Sophie and Marc Lefebvre emptied the cabinets of their grandmother's bathroom and bedroom on a Thursday afternoon. Their mother had asked them to do this part before the larger items were moved. In the bathroom they found unopened bars of soap, three bottles of perfume, and a medicine cabinet containing prescription bottles. Marc put the medications in a bag to return to the pharmacy, which accepted them for disposal. In the bedroom there was a nightstand with a reading lamp, a stack of crossword puzzle books, a magnifying glass, and two pairs of reading glasses. Sophie found a small address book in the drawer and set it aside, because their mother would need it to notify people. They folded the bed linens and stacked them on the mattress, and Marc carried the lamp to the car.

My brother and I were tasked with clearing the shed at the end of our grandmother's garden. The shed was wooden, about three meters by two, and the door stuck on the frame. Inside there were plant pots, a wheelbarrow with a flat tire, hose reels, a folding deckchair, and a set of shelves with tins of paint. My brother, Kofi, read the labels on the paint tins, and most were from the 1990s and had dried out. We checked the council website, which said paint tins could be dropped off at the recycling center on weekdays. We loaded them into the car along with the hose reels, which were cracked. The wheelbarrow only needed a new inner tube, so Kofi took it home. The deckchair went to a neighbor who had asked for it.

At seven-forty on Monday, Giorgos Antoniou unlocked the steel shutter of his hardware store and pushed it up on its rails. He switched on the lights in the order he always did: front display, aisles, back counter. The alarm panel by the door beeped, and he entered the four-digit code. He then counted the cash in the register drawer, which held two hundred euros in small notes and coins, the same as he had left on Saturday. A delivery of paint was due at nine. He checked the answering machine, which had two messages: one from a customer asking whether he stocked a specific type of hinge, and one from his supplier confirming the delivery. He wrote both down on a notepad. At eight he flipped the sign on the door from closed to open.

I own a small bakery, and on Mondays I arrive at five because the shop is closed on Sundays and there is nothing left from the weekend. The first thing I do is turn on the deck oven, which takes forty minutes to reach temperature. While it heats, I take the dough I mixed on Saturday out of the walk-in cooler. It has been fermenting slowly for two days. I divide it on the bench using a scale, at five hundred grams per loaf, and shape twenty-four loaves. My assistant, Nadia, comes in at six and starts the croissants. By six-thirty the first loaves are in the oven. I wipe down the display case and fill the price tags on the shelves. At seven I unlock the front door and the first customer, a man in a bus driver's uniform, buys two rolls.

Svetlana Ivanova opened her flower shop at eight on Monday mornings, but she arrived at seven to receive the weekly delivery from the wholesale market. The van pulled up outside at seven-ten, and the driver unloaded six buckets of cut flowers and four boxes of potted plants. Svetlana checked each item against the invoice: two buckets of roses, one of tulips, one of chrysanthemums, one of eucalyptus, and one of lilies. Everything matched. She trimmed the stems of the roses at an angle and moved them into fresh water with flower food. She placed the potted plants on the shelves by the window, where they would get the most light. At seven-fifty she swept the floor, emptied the trimmings into the compost bin in the back, and turned the sign on the door.

On Monday morning I opened the bookshop at nine-thirty, as usual. First I unlocked the front door and disabled the alarm. Then I went through the weekend's online orders, which had come in through our website. There were seven. I printed the order slips and pulled the books from the shelves, checking each one for damage. Two of the titles were out of stock, so I placed orders with the distributor and emailed the customers to say there would be a delay of about five working days. I packed the other five orders in padded mailers and stacked them by the door for the post carrier. My employee, Callum, arrived at ten and started on the new arrivals, which had been delivered on Friday. He priced each book and shelved them in the new releases section.

Mustafa Yilmaz ran a convenience store on a corner near a bus station, and on Monday mornings he opened at six. The newspaper bundles had already been dropped outside the door by the distributor. He cut the plastic straps and arranged the papers on the rack by the counter. Then he checked the refrigerators. The milk delivery from Friday had a use-by date of Tuesday, so he moved the older cartons to the front. He turned on the coffee machine and filled the paper cup dispenser. The first customer of the day, a woman in nursing scrubs, bought a coffee and a packet of gum and paid by card. At six-thirty, the bread delivery arrived, and the driver handed him a delivery note to sign. Mustafa counted the loaves in each crate before signing.

I run a bicycle repair shop, and Monday is always the busiest day for drop-offs. I opened at eight and found three bikes already locked to the rack outside with tags on their handlebars. The tags had names, phone numbers, and a short description of the problem. One needed a new chain, one had a flat rear tire, and one had a rear derailleur that was not shifting. I brought them inside and logged each one in the repair book with the date and an estimated completion time. Then I checked the parts inventory and found that I had only one chain of the right width left. I ordered five more from the supplier's website for delivery on Wednesday. At eight-thirty, a man named Desmond came in with a child's bike that needed new brake pads.

The dry cleaner's owner, Kim Soo-ah, unlocked the shop at seven on Monday. The first thing she did was switch on the steam boiler, which needed thirty minutes to build pressure. While it heated, she sorted the garments that had been dropped off on Saturday afternoon. Each item had a paper tag with a number, and she checked the tags against the ticket book. There were thirty-two items: shirts, suits, two wedding dresses in garment bags, and a set of curtains. She separated them by fabric type and placed them in labeled bins. The wedding dresses went into a separate bin for hand-finishing. At seven-thirty she ran the first load in the dry cleaning machine. A customer came in at eight to pick up a suit, and she found it on the rail by its ticket number.

I opened the pharmacy at eight-thirty. I unlocked the side door first and went in to switch off the alarm, then opened the front door and rolled up the security grille. The prescriptions waiting from the weekend were in a tray on the counter, sent electronically by the clinics on Saturday. There were nineteen. My technician, Beatriz, started filling them while I checked the refrigerator log, which records the temperature of the vaccine fridge every hour. It had stayed between three and five degrees all weekend, which was within range. I signed the log and put it back on its clipboard. Then I checked the controlled substances cabinet against the register, as required at the start of each week. The counts matched. At nine, the first patient came in to collect a refill.

Corinne Lavallée owned a small clothing boutique and opened at ten on Mondays. She arrived at nine-fifteen with a coffee and a bag of new stock she had picked up from a supplier on Sunday. She unpacked the bag behind the counter: twelve sweaters in three colors, each with a tag already attached. She entered them into the inventory system on the laptop and printed price labels. The display mannequin in the window was still wearing a summer dress, so she changed it to a wool skirt, a turtleneck, and a camel coat. She steamed the creases out of the sweaters with a handheld steamer and folded them on the table near the entrance. At nine-fifty she counted the float in the till, turned on the music, and unlocked the front door.

I opened my hardware and garden supply store at seven-thirty, and Monday is when the contractors come in. I unlocked the gate to the outdoor yard where we keep the lumber, bags of cement, and gravel. Then I went inside and turned on the computer system, which took a few minutes to start. The weekend staff had left a note listing what had sold out: two-by-fours, eight-foot lengths, and fifty-pound bags of mortar mix. I called the lumber yard and placed an order for delivery on Tuesday. The first contractor, a man named Augustin, came in at seven-forty with a list for a bathroom job. He needed tile spacers, grout, a notched trowel, and a box of drywall screws. I gathered them and rang him up on his company's account.

Abebe Tesfaye's café opened at seven on Mondays. He came in at six and turned on the espresso machine, which needed twenty minutes to heat up. He took the pastries out of the freezer and put them in the oven: twelve croissants, eight pains au chocolat, and six cinnamon rolls, all baked from frozen. While they baked, he set the chairs down from the tables and wiped each surface with a cloth and spray. He filled the milk jugs and lined them up in the small refrigerator under the counter. At six-forty he pulled two test shots of espresso and adjusted the grinder slightly finer, because the first shot had run too fast. He wrote the day's soup on the chalkboard: lentil and tomato. At seven he unlocked the door and turned on the open sign.

My shop sells sewing supplies and fabric by the meter, and I opened it at nine on Monday morning. The first thing I did was check the email inbox, where there were four questions from customers about stock. One asked whether we had a specific shade of thread, so I checked the thread wall, found it, and replied with a photo. Then I cut fabric for an online order that had come in on Sunday: two meters of navy cotton and one and a half meters of linen. I folded each length, wrapped them in tissue paper, and put them in a mailer bag. At ten, a woman named Perpetua came in to ask about the beginner quilting class that starts next week. I showed her the schedule pinned by the register and signed her up.

Every Thursday, Bernadette Kowalski volunteered for a four-hour shift at the community food bank in the basement of a church. She signed in at the front desk at nine and put on a name tag and a pair of disposable gloves. The coordinator, a man named Ignatius, assigned her to the sorting table. Donations from a weekend grocery drive were stacked in crates along the wall. Her job was to check each item's expiry date, set aside anything damaged or expired, and sort the rest into categories: canned vegetables, canned fruit, pasta and rice, cereal, and baby food. She placed each category in a labeled bin. When a bin was full, another volunteer carried it to the shelves in the distribution room. By noon she had sorted eleven crates, and she recorded the count on a clipboard.

I volunteer at the food bank on Saturday mornings, and this week I was assigned to the intake desk. Each household that comes in fills out a short form with their address and the number of people living there. I enter the information into a laptop, which shows how many visits they have made this month and which box size they qualify for. There are three sizes: small for one or two people, medium for three to five, and large for six or more. Once I confirm the size, I write it on a card and hand it to the person, who takes it to the distribution line. The morning I worked, we registered sixty-three households. At eleven-thirty the coordinator, Rosalind, asked me to count the remaining medium boxes in the back. There were fourteen.

Jarrah Williams had signed up to drive for the food bank's delivery program, which brought groceries to people who could not travel to the distribution center. On Tuesday morning he picked up his route sheet at the loading dock. It listed nine addresses in the eastern part of the city, with notes about access: one building had a broken elevator, another required a buzzer code. Two volunteers loaded his car with nine boxes, each labeled with a surname and a number. Jarrah arranged them in the trunk and back seat in the order of the route. The first stop was a ground-floor apartment, where an older man named Mr. Kaminski opened the door and asked him to put the box on the kitchen table. Jarrah did so, checked the address off the sheet, and drove to the next stop.

My first shift at the food bank was on a Wednesday afternoon. The volunteer coordinator, Esperanza, gave me a fifteen-minute orientation: where the restrooms and fire exits were, how to lift boxes safely by bending at the knees, and how the shelving was organized. Then she put me on the produce table. A local farm had donated about two hundred kilograms of potatoes, carrots, and onions. My job was to bag them into portions of roughly two kilograms each using the hanging scale. I filled a paper bag, weighed it, adjusted it by adding or removing a potato, and folded the top over. The bags went into plastic crates, eight per crate. Another volunteer, a retired teacher named Ludmila, was doing the same thing at the next table. By five o'clock we had bagged all of it.

The food bank received a pallet delivery every Monday from a regional distribution center, and Dariusz Wojcik was the volunteer who unloaded it. He had a forklift certification from his job at a warehouse, so the coordinator had asked him to come in on Monday mornings. At eight the truck backed up to the loading bay. Dariusz drove the forklift into the trailer, lifted the first pallet, and set it down in the storage area. There were five pallets: two of canned goods, one of dry pasta, one of breakfast cereal, and one of bottled water. He removed the plastic wrap from each and checked the contents against the delivery manifest. One box of canned tomatoes was dented, and he noted it on the manifest. Then he signed the driver's copy and parked the forklift.

I help out at our neighborhood food bank once a month, usually in the distribution room. On this particular Friday, I was assigned to the shelf where clients choose their items. The food bank uses a client-choice model, which means people walk through with a shopping cart and select what they need, within limits posted on each shelf. My section was canned protein: tuna, chicken, beans, and chickpeas. The sign said two items per household. My job was to keep the shelf stocked and answer questions. A woman asked whether we had any low-sodium beans, and I checked the back of the shelf, where I found six cans and gave her two. A man named Cornelius asked whether the tuna was packed in oil or water. I checked the label and told him water.

Every December the food bank ran a holiday meal program, and Yasmin Farouk had volunteered to help pack the meal boxes. Each box was supposed to contain a frozen chicken, a bag of potatoes, a can of cranberry sauce, a box of stuffing mix, two cans of green beans, and a package of rolls. The volunteers worked in an assembly line along four long tables. Yasmin was at the second station, where she added the potatoes and the cranberry sauce. The person before her, a teenager named Kwabena Mensah-Bright, added the stuffing and the green beans. At the end of the line, two people taped the boxes shut and stacked them on pallets. The frozen chickens were added last, from a refrigerated truck parked outside. By three o'clock they had packed four hundred and twenty boxes.

I had volunteered at the food bank for two years, and the manager asked me to train new volunteers on the inventory system. The system is a spreadsheet on a shared computer in the office. Each row is an item, with columns for quantity, location, and expiry date. When donations come in, someone has to enter them. When items go out, the quantities are reduced at the end of each day. On Thursday, I sat down with a new volunteer named Philippa and walked her through entering a donation of forty jars of peanut butter. We typed the item name, the quantity, the shelf code B-4, and the expiry date from the lid. Then I showed her how to sort the sheet by expiry date so that the oldest items would be distributed first.

The food bank's kitchen prepared hot lunches three days a week, and Lorenzo Bianchi volunteered there on Wednesdays. He arrived at nine to start cooking for about eighty people. The menu that day was vegetable soup, bread, and a fruit cup. He washed and chopped carrots, celery, onions, and potatoes, working through four large bags with a chef's knife. Another volunteer, a woman named Henrietta, browned the onions in a large stockpot and added the stock. Lorenzo added the rest of the vegetables, along with canned tomatoes and a handful of dried herbs. The soup simmered for an hour while he sliced six loaves of bread and portioned fruit into small plastic cups with lids. At eleven-thirty they ladled the soup into bowls and set them on trays at the serving window.

I volunteered at a mobile food bank, which was a truck that parked in the lot of a school every second Saturday. When I arrived at eight, the truck was already there, and the driver had lowered the side panels to show shelves of boxes inside. Our team of six set up folding tables in a line. Each table held a different category: produce, dairy, bread, canned goods, and hygiene products. I worked at the dairy table, where we had cartons of milk, blocks of cheese, and tubs of yogurt in insulated coolers. People came through the line with bags or carts, and I handed each household one carton of milk, one block of cheese, and two tubs of yogurt. The line started at nine and continued until about eleven-fifteen.

Pham Thi Lan volunteered at the food bank's front desk on Monday evenings, answering the phone and scheduling appointments. Most calls were from people asking about opening hours, eligibility, and what documents to bring. Lan had a script on a laminated card: the food bank was open Monday, Wednesday, and Saturday; it served anyone living in the county; and first-time visitors needed to bring proof of address, such as a utility bill. She took a call from a woman asking whether the food bank had diapers, and she checked the inventory list, which showed sizes three and four in stock. Another caller wanted to donate canned goods from a school drive and asked where to drop them off. Lan gave him the address of the loading dock and the hours it was staffed.

I was asked to help with the food bank's quarterly cleaning day. The food bank closes for one Saturday every three months so volunteers can clean and reorganize. I arrived at nine and joined a group of ten people. The coordinator, a man named Thaddeus, divided us into teams. My team was responsible for the walk-in freezer. We moved all the frozen items onto a refrigerated truck temporarily, then wiped down the shelves with a cleaning solution and scraped ice off the floor with a plastic scraper. We checked the thermometer, which showed minus eighteen degrees once the door had been closed for twenty minutes. Then we brought the items back in, arranged them by category, and wrote the date of the cleaning on the log sheet taped inside the door.

Archibald Fenwick sat in the waiting area of the hospital's outpatient clinic on a plastic chair near the window.
