He had arrived at nine-forty for a ten o'clock appointment with the orthopedic department. The receptionist had checked his name and date of birth, scanned his insurance card, and given him a numbered slip: forty-two. A screen on the wall showed the numbers being called, and it currently displayed thirty-eight. There were about twenty other people in the room. A television in the corner was showing a cooking program with the sound off and captions on. Archibald took a folded newspaper from his coat pocket and opened it to the crossword. He filled in four answers. At ten-fifteen the screen changed to forty-two, and a nurse called his name from the doorway.

I sat in the emergency department's waiting room for three hours with a cut on my left hand. It was a clean cut from a kitchen knife, and I had wrapped it in a dish towel before driving over. At triage, a nurse unwrapped it, looked at it, and said it would need a few stitches but was not urgent. She gave me a clean gauze pad and told me to keep pressure on it. The waiting room had about thirty chairs in rows, a vending machine, and a water dispenser with paper cups. A board by the triage desk listed the estimated wait time as two to four hours. I watched the people around me get called one by one. At about eleven, a doctor named Dr. Abiodun called my name, and I followed her to a cubicle.

Marisa Quintero was in the surgical waiting room on the third floor while her husband had a knee replacement. The nurse at the desk had given her a pager, like the ones used in restaurants, and told her it would buzz when the surgeon was ready to speak with her. The procedure was scheduled to take about two hours. A screen on the wall showed a list of patient codes with colored status bars: pre-op, in surgery, in recovery. Her husband's code was 4471, and his bar was purple, which meant in surgery. Marisa had brought a book and a thermos of coffee. She read two chapters. At eleven-thirty, the bar for 4471 changed to green, for recovery. Twenty minutes later the pager buzzed, and she went to the desk.

I waited in the radiology department for an MRI on my lower back. When I arrived, the receptionist asked me to fill out a safety questionnaire on a clipboard. It asked whether I had any metal implants, a pacemaker, or tattoos, and whether I had ever worked with metal grinding. I answered no to all of them and signed the bottom. Then she gave me a locker key and asked me to change into a gown in the changing room next to the waiting area. I put my clothes, phone, keys, and watch into the locker and came back out. The waiting area had six chairs and a small table with magazines. A technician named Rasmus came out after about twenty-five minutes, checked my wristband, and walked me down the corridor to the scanner room.

Ji-ho Shin brought his daughter to the pediatric emergency room after she fell off a swing at the park and her wrist began to swell. At the front desk he gave her name, date of birth, and their address, and the clerk printed a wristband for her. A triage nurse examined the wrist, gave her a dose of children's ibuprofen, and put on a temporary splint. Then they were sent to the waiting room, which had colorful chairs, a play area with blocks and a bead maze, and a fish tank. His daughter sat on his lap and watched the fish. Ji-ho checked his phone and sent a message to his wife with the name of the hospital. After forty minutes, a nurse called them into an examination room and said an X-ray had been ordered.

I sat in the waiting area of the blood test clinic at seven in the morning, because my doctor had ordered fasting bloodwork and I wanted to get it done before breakfast. I took a number from the machine at the entrance: 117. The display above the counter showed 109. There were eight people ahead of me. The room had rows of chairs facing a wall with three numbered doors. Each door opened into a small room with a phlebotomist. The process for each patient seemed to take about four minutes. I read the posters on the walls while I waited. One explained how to prepare for a glucose tolerance test, and another listed the clinic's opening hours. At seven-thirty-five my number was called to door two, and I went in and rolled up my sleeve.

Olufemi Bankole was waiting in the cardiology department for a routine echocardiogram that his doctor had ordered as part of an annual check. He had been told to arrive fifteen minutes early, so he got there at one-forty-five. The waiting room was small, with eight chairs and a coat rack. A wall-mounted dispenser held hand sanitizer, and a sign asked patients to switch their phones to silent. Olufemi took out a pen and a small notebook in which he had written three questions for the doctor: whether he should continue his current medication, whether he could resume running, and when the next check would be. He read through them once. A man next to him was reading a printed list of his own medications. At two-ten, a sonographer named Ms. Takahashi called his name.

I was waiting in the maternity ward's family room while my sister was in labor. The nurses had said it could be several hours. The room had a sofa, two armchairs, a small kitchen counter with a kettle, and a cupboard stocked with tea bags and packets of biscuits. There was a sign asking visitors to wash their mugs after use. My brother-in-law came out every hour or so to give updates, which were mostly about the number of centimeters and the timing of contractions. I made tea, read the hospital's visitor leaflet twice, and charged my phone at an outlet next to the window. Outside, the parking lot was half full. At around four in the morning, my brother-in-law came out and said the baby had been born and that both were fine.

Svetozar Marković brought his mother to the hospital for a scheduled cataract operation. After she was admitted to the day surgery unit, a nurse told him the procedure and recovery would take about three hours and directed him to the waiting room on the ground floor. The room had a row of windows facing the hospital garden and a coffee machine that accepted coins. Svetozar bought a coffee and sat in a chair by the window. He opened his laptop and answered work emails using the hospital's guest Wi-Fi, whose password was written on a card by the door. At noon he walked to the cafeteria and bought a sandwich. At one-fifteen the nurse called his phone to say his mother was ready for discharge, and he went up to the unit to collect her.

I spent the afternoon in a hospital waiting room while my father had a colonoscopy. It was a routine screening, and he had been told it would take about forty-five minutes plus time in recovery. Since he would be sedated, he needed someone to drive him home, which is why I was there. The waiting room was beside the endoscopy unit and had about fifteen chairs, a water cooler, and a rack of pamphlets about digestive health. I read a pamphlet about fiber intake and then worked on a spreadsheet on my laptop. A nurse came out at intervals to call family members of other patients. After about an hour and a quarter, she called my name and took me to the recovery area, where my father was sitting up and drinking apple juice.

Ananya Bose waited in the oncology department's waiting area for her monthly follow-up appointment. She had been coming every four weeks for a year, and she knew the routine. First she checked in at the kiosk by scanning the barcode on her appointment letter. Then she went to the phlebotomy room for a blood draw, which took five minutes. After that, she returned to the waiting area, where the blood results would be processed before her consultation. The room had large windows, armchairs, and a volunteer pushing a cart with tea and coffee. Ananya took a cup of tea and sat in her usual chair near the aquarium. She had brought her knitting and worked on the sleeve of a cardigan. At eleven, the nurse called her into the consultation room.

I sat in the waiting room of the hospital's physical therapy department with my left arm in a sling. It was my first session after shoulder surgery six weeks earlier. The receptionist asked me to fill out a form rating my pain and range of motion on a scale of one to ten, and I gave it back to her. The room had a dozen chairs, a rack of exercise bands hanging on the wall for sale, and a poster showing shoulder stretches. Through a glass partition I could see the therapy gym, where several patients were working with therapists on mats and with weights. One man was walking between parallel bars. At three o'clock a physical therapist named Bartholomew came out with a clipboard, called my name, and led me to a treatment table.
